processes.description: Ahead of each month, the contract administrator for Houston Pipe Line compiles a report of contract assignments, terminations, expirations and contracts still in process, and mails it as an attachment to schedulers, traders and logistics staff, who read it for changes affecting their deals. A later round is a dated status snapshot sent near month end. When a month's report is missed, the sender owns up and catches up in the next mailing.
steps: Pull the contract changes for the coming month from the contract system.
Sort them into assignments, terminations, expirations and contracts in process.
Build the report spreadsheet and date it with the as-of time.
Mail the report as an attachment to the distribution of schedulers and logistics staff.
Recipients check the report for contracts that affect their nominations and deals.

stalls.summary: A month's report was skipped by accident and only noticed afterwards, so recipients went without the contract changes for that month until a catch-up mailing.

automation.approach: Generate the assignment, termination and expiration report directly from the contract system on a fixed schedule, with a calendar reminder and a send checklist so no month is skipped, and a standard cover note naming the period and as-of time.
automation.rationale: The report is the same layout every month and the one failure the mail shows is a skipped month, which a dated monthly checklist covering pull, sort, build and send prevents most directly.

work_estimate.rationale: Most of the time goes to pulling contract changes, classifying them into the report's categories and formatting the spreadsheet with an as-of date; around 60 minutes for a pipeline's monthly contract list, longer when a month must be caught up. The pull and layout are repeatable and could be generated, leaving review of the entries.

processes.description: Staff and managers email HR or an assistant to change an employee's record or pay: setting up operating companies or system access for new people, adding people left off a roster, switching a parking benefit to a bus pass, stopping a charitable payroll deduction, or confirming whether departed employees get an extra payment. HR in turn sends surveys and membership questionnaires to fill out and return by a stated deadline. Each request is looked up, the record changed or the answer confirmed, and the requester told.
steps: An employee or manager emails a record, pay or benefit change, or HR sends out a form to complete.
The handler looks up the employee's current record or the policy in question.
The handler enters the change or confirms the answer with HR or payroll.
Missing people or access are added to the roster or system.
The requester is told the result, and completed forms are collected back.

stalls.summary: A manager needed a policy answer for a former employee who had called, and had to ask HR to let him know when they had something.
People were left off a distribution or missing from the system, so a second request was needed to set them up.
A roster check reached a manager who replied he managed no one in that pool, so the request went to the wrong person.

automation.approach: Route record and benefit changes through one request form with fields for employee, change type and effective date, feeding a tracked queue; keep roster checks against the HR system as a generated list sent only to each person's actual manager.
automation.rationale: The requests are short and varied but share the same fields; a standard form removes the back-and-forth over missing people and misrouted roster checks, and gives the requester a status to look at instead of asking.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round is a single record lookup and change or a policy confirmation: switching a benefit, stopping a deduction, adding a missing person to a system, or filling in a short survey. Around 15 minutes of lookup and entry; a request form and queue would take over part of the intake and entry, while the policy answers stay with people.

processes.description: Settlements and accounting staff find a mismatch between a counterparty invoice or payment and the deal as booked in Sitara: a different price, an unpriced or wrong index, unactualized volumes, a deal that should be netted, or an invoice for gas never paid. They ask the scheduler or trader to verify the deal, correct the ticket or say what to bill, sometimes pulling trader tape recordings or checking published market prices for power disputes. Once the deal is corrected, the invoice is paid or rebilled before the payment date.
steps: Settlements notices an invoice, payment or price that does not match the deal in Sitara.
They email the scheduler or trader with the deal number and the two figures.
The trader or scheduler checks the deal terms, volumes or published price, sometimes pulling tapes.
The ticket is corrected in Sitara or the counterparty is told the correct price.
Settlements reruns the invoice or payment and confirms before the due date.
Unresolved items are chased or escalated to the counterparty.

stalls.summary: Settlements waits on the scheduler or trader to verify deals, chasing with follow-ups while payment dates approach.
Counterparties do not return calls about outstanding payments or disputed deals.
Confusion over who handles a deal: requests go to the wrong desk or person and are redirected.
Sitara itself blocks fixes: a ticket could not be opened to correct swing pricing, and the system held two prices for one day.
Volumes not yet actualized leave nothing in volume management to settle against.
Staff departures leave items open, with a handler trying to finish what they can before leaving.

contradictions.summary: Invoice and system prices disagree for the same deal: a counterparty billed one price while Sitara showed another, and Sitara held two prices for the same day.
A price change believed final was not the final price for the deal, and a counterparty changed its price mid-dispute.

Ownership of disputed deals is stated differently: one sender was told another person handled the deal, another says a deal belongs to a different desk, and a third asks that all monetized questions go through one person.
Practice conflicts on contacting customers: staff emailed counterparties about disputes while a manager told them not to send dispute emails to customers.

automation.approach: Run a daily match of counterparty invoices against Sitara deal prices and volumes, listing each variance with deal number, both figures, the responsible desk and the payment due date, and send it to the owning scheduler or trader with a standard query. Track each variance to closure so follow-ups and escalations come from the list rather than ad hoc chasing.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same question asked in different words: this invoice says one price, Sitara says another, which is right. A standard variance query with the deal number, both figures, due date and owner cuts the clarification loops and misrouting, and a matching report finds the mismatches before they become payment-day emergencies.

work_estimate.rationale: Each round involves finding the deal in Sitara, comparing invoice and booked price or volume, checking the index or published price, correcting the ticket and rerunning the invoice; power disputes add checking risk records or pulling tapes. Around 45 minutes for a single-deal price fix, up to two hours where tapes or several deals are involved. Matching and variance listing are repeatable; the judgement on the right price stays with people.
